before: A finite verb hosts at most one subject index and one object index. No additional personal prefix or suffix is possible regardless of how many semantic participants the predicate involves. The restriction is most visible in three-place predicates: with kore 'give', recipient and theme cannot each receive an overt index. When both are third person, neither is indexed and both surface as bare noun phrases ; .
after: A verb permits person indexing of at most two arguments: a subject and one object . A three-place verb such as kore 'give' therefore has only one object-indexing position for its recipient and theme. Third-person arguments have no overt person marker . In the following example both objects are expressed as bare noun phrases; either can be omitted when recoverable from context .
evidence: Satō 2023:39 n.3 limits indexed arguments to two. Nakagawa 2024:166,170 gives third-person zero forms;127 ex.11a–c explicitly allows either object NP to be omitted. Original p127 inspected.

before: The ceiling also determines how reflexive and reciprocal derivations interact with personal marking. Once yay-, si-, or u- occupies the internal argument position as part of a derived stem, the verb is indexed according to its derived valence; a separate object index for the same participant would exceed the cap and is ungrammatical ; . Satō uses this two-index restriction to argue that a zero third-person index must be posited in the paradigm, so that the cap is stateable uniformly, in disagreement with Nakagawa's earlier position that third person has no affix ; ; ‹contested›.
after:
Reflexive and reciprocal prefixes belong to the derivational stem. In their valence-reducing uses, yay-, si-, and u- reduce the number of arguments by one . Person marking then follows the derived verb's valence. A two-place base becomes intransitive, while a three-place base can remain transitive: Satō lists ko-ruska as three-place and yay-ko-ruska as transitive . The derived transitive retains an object-indexing position. Nakagawa's template places person indexes outside these derivational prefixes .

The analysis of third person remains disputed. Satō argues for a zero third-person index using the absence of causative forms that would index three participants. He contrasts this with Nakagawa's 2001 analysis, in which third person has no affix ‹contested›. This argument concerns the number of indexed participants; the reflexive and reciprocal prefixes themselves are derivational elements.
evidence: Nakagawa2024:185–188,210 distinguishes nominal derivation and outer person layer; Satō2023:40 explicitly three-place ko-ruska vs transitive yay-ko-ruska. Satō39 n.3 disputes Nakagawa2001:48, not Nakagawa2024:169; treats absent causative forms as probably impossible, so do not assert absolute impossibility.

before: The ditransitive evidence bears directly on alignment. Satō argues that the object index in three-place verbs such as kore 'give' ordinarily identifies the human recipient while the theme stays unindexed — a secundative pattern in the indexing slot ; . Nakagawa describes the same verbs through valency, with two bare object phrases when both are third person . Both accounts converge on the generalization that a verb hosts at most one subject index and one object index; the difference is whether the unfilled third-person position contains a zero marker ‹contested›.
after: With kore 'give', Satō treats recipient indexing as the ordinary secundative pattern while acknowledging exceptional theme indexing . Nakagawa's examples show both objects as bare noun phrases and allow either to be omitted when recoverable from context . evidence: Satō2023:39n3 explicitly disputing Nakagawa2001;40n5 defaults and exceptions. Nakagawa2024:127 bare NPs and contextual omission. Avoid representing differences as exhausted by a single issue.
